books.title: Science
books.edition: Reprint 2026-27 (First Edition December 2006; Revised Edition October 2022; reprinted January 2026)

source.method: chapter titles from the book's Contents page; topics from each chapter PDF's numbered section headings (a parent heading that is only a short lead-in to its subsections is not a separate topic; Summary/Exercises are not topics)

topics.title: Chemical Equations
objectives: Student can name the observations (change in state, colour, temperature, evolution of a gas) that show a chemical reaction has taken place
Student can write a word equation identifying reactants and products, as for magnesium burning in oxygen
visualIdeas: magnesium ribbon burning with a dazzling white flame into white magnesium oxide powder
reactants on the left, an arrow, products on the right

topics.title: Writing a Chemical Equation
objectives: Student can convert a word equation into a skeletal chemical equation using chemical formulae
Student can explain why a skeletal equation such as Mg + O2 -> MgO is not yet balanced
visualIdeas: word equation turning into a formula equation line by line

topics.title: Balanced Chemical Equations
objectives: Student can state that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, so atoms of each element must be equal on both sides
Student can balance an equation step by step, as for Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2
Student can add state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) and reaction conditions to an equation
visualIdeas: a two-pan balance with atoms counted on each side
a table counting atoms of each element before and after balancing

topics.title: Combination Reaction
objectives: Student can define a combination reaction as one in which a single product forms from two or more reactants
Student can explain the reaction of quicklime with water to form slaked lime and why it releases heat
Student can distinguish exothermic reactions and give examples such as burning of natural gas and respiration
visualIdeas: calcium oxide in a beaker of water with a hand feeling heat
two reactant boxes merging into one product box

topics.title: Decomposition Reaction
objectives: Student can define a decomposition reaction as a single reactant breaking down into simpler products
Student can distinguish thermal decomposition, electrolysis of water, and light-driven decomposition of silver chloride
Student can explain why decomposition reactions are generally endothermic and give the use of silver bromide in black and white photography
visualIdeas: ferrous sulphate crystals heated in a boiling tube, colour change and smell of burning sulphur
electrolysis of water with hydrogen volume twice the oxygen volume

topics.title: Displacement Reaction
objectives: Student can explain why an iron nail placed in copper sulphate solution turns brownish and the blue colour fades
Student can identify a displacement reaction as a more reactive element displacing a less reactive one from its compound
visualIdeas: iron nail in blue copper sulphate solution turning brown over time

topics.title: Double Displacement Reaction
objectives: Student can describe the white precipitate of barium sulphate formed when sodium sulphate and barium chloride solutions are mixed
Student can define a double displacement reaction as an exchange of ions between reactants and define a precipitation reaction
visualIdeas: two solutions poured together forming a white precipitate
ion partners swapping places

topics.title: Oxidation and Reduction
objectives: Student can explain the black copper oxide formed on heating copper as oxidation and its reaction with hydrogen as reduction
Student can define oxidation as gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen and reduction as loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen
Student can identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in a redox reaction such as ZnO + C -> Zn + CO
visualIdeas: copper powder in a china dish turning black on heating
arrows labelling oxygen gained and oxygen lost in one equation

topics.title: Corrosion
objectives: Student can explain corrosion as a metal being attacked by substances around it such as moisture and acids
Student can describe examples: black coating on silver, green coating on copper and rusting of iron, and why corrosion is costly
visualIdeas: a rusted iron gate beside a tarnished silver spoon and a green copper vessel

topics.title: Rancidity
objectives: Student can explain rancidity as the oxidation of fats and oils that changes their smell and taste
Student can describe ways to prevent rancidity: antioxidants, airtight containers, and flushing chip bags with nitrogen
visualIdeas: a chips packet being filled with nitrogen gas

topics.title: Acids and Bases in the Laboratory
objectives: Student can use litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein to tell acids from bases
Student can explain olfactory indicators such as onion, vanilla and clove oil that change smell in acid or base
visualIdeas: test tubes of acids and bases with litmus colours shown
a table of indicator colours in acid and base

topics.title: How do Acids and Bases React with Metals?
objectives: Student can describe how an acid reacts with zinc to give a salt and hydrogen gas, tested with a burning candle
Student can describe the reaction of sodium hydroxide with zinc to form sodium zincate and hydrogen
visualIdeas: zinc granules in dilute sulphuric acid with bubbles collected into soap bubbles that pop near a flame

topics.title: How do Metal Carbonates and Metal Hydrogencarbonates React with Acids?
objectives: Student can write the general reaction: metal carbonate or hydrogencarbonate + acid -> salt + carbon dioxide + water
Student can describe how carbon dioxide turns lime water milky and how excess gas makes it clear again
visualIdeas: gas from a test tube bubbling through lime water turning milky

topics.title: How do Acids and Bases React with each other?
objectives: Student can explain neutralisation as acid + base -> salt + water
Student can describe how phenolphthalein shows neutralisation when acid is added to pink sodium hydroxide solution
visualIdeas: pink solution turning colourless drop by drop

topics.title: Reaction of Metallic Oxides with Acids
objectives: Student can describe copper oxide dissolving in dilute hydrochloric acid to form a blue-green copper chloride solution
Student can explain why metallic oxides are called basic oxides
visualIdeas: black copper oxide powder dissolving into a blue-green solution

topics.title: Reaction of a Non-metallic Oxide with Base
objectives: Student can describe carbon dioxide reacting with calcium hydroxide to form salt and water
Student can conclude that non-metallic oxides are acidic in nature
visualIdeas: side-by-side cards: metal oxide is basic, non-metal oxide is acidic

topics.title: What do all Acids and all Bases have in Common?
objectives: Student can describe the activity showing that acid solutions conduct electricity while glucose and alcohol solutions do not
Student can explain that acids produce H+ ions in solution, which gives them their acidic properties
visualIdeas: a bulb glowing in a circuit dipped into dilute HCl but not into glucose solution

topics.title: What Happens to an Acid or a Base in a Water Solution?
objectives: Student can explain why dry HCl gas does not change the colour of dry litmus paper while wet litmus does, so acids give H+ ions only in water
Student can explain that acids give hydronium ions (H3O+) and bases give hydroxide ions (OH-) in water
Student can define alkalis as bases that are soluble in water
Student can explain why the acid must be added slowly to water while diluting, and not water to acid
visualIdeas: acid being poured slowly into a beaker of water with a warning sign

topics.title: How Strong are Acid or Base Solutions?
objectives: Student can use the pH scale from 0 to 14 to classify solutions as acidic, neutral or basic
Student can use universal indicator colours to estimate pH
Student can distinguish strong and weak acids and bases by the concentration of H+ or OH- ions they produce
visualIdeas: a coloured pH scale strip with common substances placed on it

topics.title: Importance of pH in Everyday Life
objectives: Student can explain why living things survive only in a narrow pH range, with acid rain as an example
Student can explain how antacids relieve acidity and how tooth decay starts below pH 5.5
Student can describe self-defence by bee stings and nettle leaves and how they are treated with a mild base
visualIdeas: a mouth with pH dropping below 5.5 near teeth
a bee sting being treated with baking soda

topics.title: Family of Salts
objectives: Student can write the formulae of salts and identify the acid and base each came from
Student can group salts into families sharing the same positive or negative radical
visualIdeas: a grid of salts sorted by sodium salts and chloride salts

topics.title: pH of Salts
objectives: Student can explain that salts of a strong acid and strong base are neutral
Student can explain that salts of a strong acid and weak base are acidic and salts of a strong base and weak acid are basic
visualIdeas: three beakers of salt solutions with pH paper showing neutral, acidic and basic

topics.title: Chemicals from Common Salt
objectives: Student can describe the chlor-alkali process producing sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen and their uses
Student can describe the preparation and uses of bleaching powder
Student can explain the uses of baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) and washing soda (sodium carbonate decahydrate)
visualIdeas: an electrolysis cell of brine with chlorine at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode
a cake rising because of baking powder releasing carbon dioxide

topics.title: Are the Crystals of Salts really Dry?
objectives: Student can explain water of crystallisation using blue copper sulphate turning white on heating
Student can describe how Plaster of Paris is made from gypsum and why it sets hard when mixed with water
Student can list uses of Plaster of Paris such as supporting fractured bones and making toys
visualIdeas: blue crystals turning white when heated and blue again when water is added
a plaster cast on an arm

topics.title: Physical Properties: Metals
objectives: Student can describe the physical properties of metals: lustre, hardness, malleability, ductility and conduction of heat and electricity
Student can name exceptions such as sodium and potassium being soft and mercury being liquid
visualIdeas: a metal sheet being hammered thin and a wire drawn out

topics.title: Physical Properties: Non-metals
objectives: Student can describe the physical properties of non-metals and name examples such as carbon, sulphur, iodine and oxygen
Student can name exceptions such as iodine having lustre and graphite conducting electricity
Student can classify elements as metals or non-metals using their properties
visualIdeas: a sorting chart of elements into metals and non-metals

topics.title: What happens when Metals are burnt in Air?
objectives: Student can explain that metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides
Student can describe amphoteric oxides such as aluminium oxide and zinc oxide that react with both acids and bases
visualIdeas: a magnesium ribbon burning to a white oxide

topics.title: What happens when Metals react with Water?
objectives: Student can compare how potassium and sodium react violently with cold water, calcium less violently and magnesium with hot water
Student can explain that aluminium, iron and zinc react only with steam and lead, copper, silver and gold do not react
visualIdeas: metals arranged by how vigorously they react with water

topics.title: What happens when Metals react with Acids?
objectives: Student can explain that metals react with dilute acids to give a salt and hydrogen gas
Student can explain why hydrogen is not evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid, except with magnesium and manganese in very dilute acid
Student can describe aqua regia and its ability to dissolve gold and platinum
visualIdeas: test tubes of metals in dilute acid with different bubbling rates

topics.title: How do Metals react with Solutions of other Metal Salts?
objectives: Student can explain that a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution
Student can predict whether a displacement will occur from the relative reactivity of two metals
visualIdeas: a copper wire in silver nitrate solution growing silver crystals

topics.title: The Reactivity Series
objectives: Student can describe the reactivity series as a list of metals in decreasing order of activity
Student can use the series to predict reactions of metals with water, acids and salt solutions
visualIdeas: a vertical ladder of metals from potassium at the top to gold at the bottom

topics.title: How do Metals and Non-metals React?
objectives: Student can explain the formation of sodium chloride and magnesium chloride by transfer of electrons
Student can draw electron-dot structures for ionic compounds
Student can define ionic (electrovalent) compounds
visualIdeas: electron-dot diagram of Na giving one electron to Cl
shells of noble gases showing stable octets

topics.title: Properties of Ionic Compounds
objectives: Student can describe physical properties of ionic compounds: solid, hard, brittle and with high melting and boiling points
Student can explain why ionic compounds dissolve in water and conduct electricity in solution or molten state
visualIdeas: a crystal lattice of alternating positive and negative ions

topics.title: Occurrence of Metals
objectives: Student can name the earth's crust and sea water (with soluble salts such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride) as sources of metals
Student can distinguish minerals from ores: ores are minerals with a high enough percentage of a metal to extract it profitably
visualIdeas: a layered earth crust showing ore deposits

topics.title: Extraction of Metals
objectives: Student can explain why metals low in the activity series, such as gold, silver, platinum and copper, are often found free in nature
Student can group metals by reactivity into those at the bottom, middle and top of the activity series
Student can outline the steps of extracting a metal from its ore
visualIdeas: a flow chart from ore to pure metal

topics.title: Enrichment of Ores
objectives: Student can explain gangue as the impurities mixed with ores
Student can explain that ores are enriched by removing gangue using differences in physical or chemical properties
visualIdeas: ore being separated from sand and soil

topics.title: Extracting Metals Low in the Activity Series
objectives: Student can explain how mercury is obtained by heating cinnabar in air
Student can explain how copper is obtained from copper sulphide by heating
visualIdeas: cinnabar heated to release mercury droplets

topics.title: Extracting Metals in the Middle of the Activity Series
objectives: Student can distinguish roasting of sulphide ores and calcination of carbonate ores
Student can explain reduction of metal oxides with carbon and the thermit reaction used to join railway tracks
visualIdeas: a thermit reaction with molten iron flowing between rail ends

topics.title: Extracting Metals towards the Top of the Activity Series
objectives: Student can explain why highly reactive metals such as sodium, magnesium and aluminium cannot be obtained by reducing their oxides with carbon
Student can describe electrolytic reduction of molten chlorides, with metal at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
visualIdeas: electrolysis cell for molten sodium chloride

topics.title: Refining of Metals
objectives: Student can describe electrolytic refining of copper with impure metal as anode and pure metal as cathode
Student can explain what anode mud is
visualIdeas: impure copper anode thinning while the pure cathode grows

topics.title: Corrosion
objectives: Student can describe the corrosion of silver, copper and iron
Student can describe the activity showing that both air and water are needed for iron to rust
visualIdeas: three test tubes with nails in dry air, boiled water under oil and ordinary water

topics.title: Prevention of Corrosion
objectives: Student can list ways to prevent rusting: painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising, chrome plating, anodising and making alloys
Student can explain alloys such as steel, brass, bronze and solder and why pure gold is alloyed for jewellery
visualIdeas: a galvanised iron sheet with a zinc coat
an alloy shown as a mixture of two kinds of atoms

topics.title: Bonding in Carbon - The Covalent Bond
objectives: Student can explain why carbon cannot easily gain or lose four electrons and instead shares electrons
Student can draw electron-dot structures for hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and methane molecules showing single, double and triple bonds
Student can describe properties of covalent compounds: low melting and boiling points and poor conduction of electricity
Student can describe diamond, graphite and fullerenes as allotropes of carbon
visualIdeas: electron-dot diagram of methane with four shared pairs
diamond 3D lattice next to graphite hexagonal layers

topics.title: Versatile Nature of Carbon
objectives: Student can explain catenation as the ability of carbon to form bonds with other carbon atoms
Student can explain tetravalency and how strong carbon bonds make compounds stable
visualIdeas: a long chain of carbon atoms linked like beads

topics.title: Saturated and Unsaturated Carbon Compounds
objectives: Student can draw structures of ethane, ethene and ethyne
Student can distinguish saturated compounds (single bonds) from unsaturated compounds (double or triple bonds)
visualIdeas: ethane, ethene, ethyne structures side by side

topics.title: Chains, Branches and Rings
objectives: Student can draw straight-chain and branched structures of butane (structural isomers)
Student can describe cyclic compounds such as cyclohexane and benzene
Student can define hydrocarbons, alkanes, alkenes and alkynes
visualIdeas: butane and isobutane drawn with the same formula
a benzene ring

topics.title: Will you be my Friend?
objectives: Student can explain that carbon bonds with heteroatoms such as halogens, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur
Student can identify functional groups such as halo, alcohol, aldehyde, ketone and carboxylic acid
visualIdeas: a carbon chain with different functional groups attached at the end

topics.title: Homologous Series
objectives: Student can define a homologous series as compounds with the same functional group differing by CH2
Student can explain how physical properties change gradually and chemical properties stay similar in a series
visualIdeas: a ladder of alcohols each step adding CH2

topics.title: Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds
objectives: Student can name carbon compounds by counting carbon atoms and adding the prefix or suffix of the functional group
Student can name compounds such as bromopropane, propanal, propanone and propanoic acid
visualIdeas: a naming flow chart: count carbons, find functional group, add suffix

topics.title: Combustion
objectives: Student can explain that carbon and its compounds burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide, heat and light
Student can explain why saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame and unsaturated ones with a sooty yellow flame
visualIdeas: a blue gas stove flame next to a sooty yellow flame

topics.title: Oxidation
objectives: Student can describe the oxidation of alcohols to carboxylic acids by alkaline potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate
Student can define oxidising agents
visualIdeas: purple permanganate decolourising when added to warm ethanol

topics.title: Addition Reaction
objectives: Student can explain hydrogenation of unsaturated hydrocarbons in the presence of nickel or palladium catalysts
Student can explain the hydrogenation of vegetable oils and why oils with unsaturated fatty acids are healthier
visualIdeas: a double bond opening as two hydrogen atoms are added

topics.title: Substitution Reaction
objectives: Student can explain the substitution of hydrogen atoms in methane by chlorine in sunlight
Student can contrast substitution with addition
visualIdeas: hydrogen atoms in methane being swapped for chlorine one by one

topics.title: Properties of Ethanol
objectives: Student can describe the physical properties and uses of ethanol
Student can describe the reaction of ethanol with sodium and its dehydration with concentrated sulphuric acid to form ethene
Student can explain the harmful effects of drinking alcohol
visualIdeas: ethanol and sodium reaction releasing hydrogen bubbles

topics.title: Properties of Ethanoic Acid
objectives: Student can describe ethanoic acid (acetic acid) and vinegar and why glacial acetic acid freezes in cold weather
Student can describe esterification and saponification
Student can describe reactions of ethanoic acid with bases, carbonates and hydrogencarbonates
visualIdeas: a test tube warmed to make a sweet-smelling ester

topics.title: Soaps and Detergents
objectives: Student can explain how soap molecules form micelles with ionic ends facing water and carbon chains trapping oil
Student can explain why soap forms scum in hard water and why detergents work in hard water
visualIdeas: a micelle with tails holding an oil drop in the centre
two test tubes with soap in soft and hard water showing foam and scum

topics.title: What are Life Processes?
objectives: Student can explain that maintenance processes such as nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion keep living things alive
Student can explain why molecular movement is a sign of life
visualIdeas: a dog sleeping with arrows showing processes still going on inside

topics.title: Autotrophic Nutrition
objectives: Student can write the equation of photosynthesis and describe its three events: absorbing light, splitting water and reducing carbon dioxide

a variegated leaf stained with iodine showing starch only in green parts

topics.title: Heterotrophic Nutrition

visualIdeas: bread mould growing on bread
a cuscuta vine on a host plant

topics.title: How do Organisms obtain their Nutrition?

topics.title: Nutrition in Human Beings
objectives: Student can trace the path of food through the alimentary canal from mouth to anus

a close-up of villi on the small intestine wall

topics.title: Respiration
objectives: Student can compare aerobic and anaerobic breakdown of glucose in yeast, muscle cells and mitochondria

topics.title: Transportation in Human Beings

visualIdeas: a schematic of the heart with oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in two colours

topics.title: Transportation in Plants

topics.title: Excretion in Human Beings

topics.title: Excretion in Plants
objectives: Student can explain how plants get rid of excess water and oxygen and store wastes in old leaves, vacuoles, resins and gums

topics.title: Animals - Nervous System

topics.title: What happens in Reflex Actions?

topics.title: Human Brain
